editorial.headline: Non-Residential Real Estate, With a Bali Warning Flag
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 68129 covers non-residential property operation and development, nationally open to full foreign ownership while Bali is marked for a proposed PMA closure.
editorial.body:
KBLI 68129 concerns the business of making non-residential real estate available, operating it, or developing it. Its scope reaches buildings held in ownership or lease, including other non-residential premises and data centres. It also embraces the development of non-residential building projects, whether the developer intends to operate them directly or sell them. Factory leasing belongs within the activity too, whether machinery and equipment are included or not. Even the rental of non-residential rooftops—for example, for solar-panel installations—sits within the stated scope.

The practical thread is property as an operating asset or development project, rather than a single type of tenant or building. A business may be earning from the use of premises it owns or leases, bringing a new non-residential project into operation, preparing it for sale, or leasing industrial space and associated equipment. The activity is open across the full recorded scale range: micro, small, medium, and large enterprises. That breadth matters because the code describes the nature of the real-estate activity, not a narrow company size or one fixed commercial format.

Nationally, the PMA position is open, with a maximum foreign ownership ceiling of 100%. In plain terms, the record permits a fully foreign-owned structure at the national level for this activity. Bali requires a more careful reading. The code is not marked as blocked for PMA registration in Bali today, but its Bali status is recorded as a proposed closure for PMA in the real-estate field. That is a serious directional signal, not the same thing as a current block.

The record also notes a permanent, island-wide Bali moratorium on PMA registration for all low- and medium-low-risk KBLI activities. It does not state this activity's risk classification or identify that moratorium as the present basis for blocking this code. The honest position is therefore precise: nationally the activity is fully open to foreign ownership; in Bali, it is not presently marked blocked in this record, yet it carries a proposed-PMA-closure status that should not be treated as a settled invitation.
